Listen, I’m not saying Cliff is a bad guy, but my pharmacist is about to go out of business because of him. Here is a draft of that story, punch-up comedian style. Feel free to post this on your socials—it’s got that "relatable academic trauma" vibe that usually does numbers. The Cure for Insomnia (Or: Why My Pharmacist Hates Cliff) I’ve been on prescription-strength melatonin for years, right? My blood is basically 40% cherry-flavored sleep aid. I thought I was a medical mystery—a man whose brain simply refused to log off. Then I met Cliff. Cliff doesn’t give lectures; he performs "auditory anesthesia." His voice isn’t a human voice—it’s the sound of a dial-up modem trying to connect in a rainstorm. It’s the sonic equivalent of watching beige paint dry in slow motion. Last week, I walked into Cliff’s room, he said, "Good morning, class, let's look at the sub-sections of paragraph B," and I was out. I didn’t just nap; I entered a coma so deep I saw my ancestors. My Fitbit actually sent a notification to my emergency contacts because it thought I had passed away. I’ve officially cancelled my prescription. Why pay a $20 co-pay for pills when I can just sit in the back row of Cliff's class for free? He is a biological miracle. If we could bottle his energy, we could solve the world’s stress levels in a weekend, mostly because everyone would be unconscious. The only problem? Anwar. See, I actually want to pass Course 330. Anwar is the problem because he’s actually... engaging? He’s funny, he’s got energy, he makes 330 feel like a Netflix special. I’m sitting there in Anwar’s class, wide awake, learning things, and laughing. It’s disgusting. I’m actually retaining information. So now I have a system: I go to Anwar to pass the degree. I go to Cliff to achieve the deepest REM cycle known to man. If you see me sprinting from Anwar’s room to Cliff’s, don’t worry. I’m just heading to my bedroom.

He's just plain terrible. While I'm happy I took the class and I learned a great deal, none of this is thanks to Pete. He's a flat-out terrible lecturer, and doesn't seem to have much going on between the ears. The projects are helpful as an introduction to kernel development, but Pete's name is nowhere to be found on the projects, nor on GeekOS (the class's operating system). 80% of what I learned in this class was from the textbook and the projects, both of which can be found for free online. The exams are awful. They test you on almost entirely minutia rather than your true understanding of the concepts. It makes no difference in real life if you can recall the exact semantics of a file system, as documentation is more accurate than memory 100% of the time. Almost all of the points I lost in the class were from exams, and I didn't even care toward the end of the class. I ended about half a point under an A-. One of the terms we were asked to define on the exam was not on any course slides, nor in the textbook. On one occasion, Pete himself had a solution incorrect in his answer key. He also, as another reviewer has mentioned, asked ChatGPT to generate him lecture material without so much as proofreading it. This class made me realize that I'm just about done with academics, and I'm now planning to graduate early. This class is an absolute joke, and the incompetency on display here has opened my eyes to how out-of-touch college departments are. Students are paying thousands of dollars in tuition a year, and yet we receive half-assed lectures from a man with maybe one brain cell in his head. You can learn all of this online if you have the motivation. Get your piece of paper, get out, and write some free and open source software. Do some good for the world, lest you become a living zombie inhabiting the dying wasteland of a university like Peter Keleher.

I would only recommend this class if you have a light semester or elite ball time management skills. - Marsh uses a flipped classroom, where he demos random stuff during class and makes you watch videos on your own. The videos are far from enough to do the projects, but you can't just skip them and self study, because there's a Canvas quiz for each one. - For the first 2 projects, there's a "follow up" where you live code in front of a TA. The coding tasks themselves aren't too bad, but the logistics are awful. There was a period where they ran out of appointments, and various announcements from Marsh and different TAs contradicted each other. It felt like they hardly communicated with each other and didn't coordinate plans at all. - He uses "standards-based grading," where grades are based on checklists of assignment statuses. For example, you need x projects at 100%, x writeups at excellent, x writeups at sufficient, etc. This made things ambiguous when you didn't match checklists perfectly and were between letter grades. FWIW, the class content is quite interesting imo and Marsh seems like a nice guy. He just has some really *creative* ideas on how to run a class.

TLDR: Prof's okay, course is really bad. You will learn nothing, buts its an ez A. Worst course I've taken IN MY LIFE, not just in college. My 8th grade art lessons were better. Pros: 2 reasons to take it: ez A, or you're in the ML track. PS: Im not saying Regli is a bad professor, I never went to the lectures (watched recordings though). He is very kind, flexible, and willing to accommodate students; he genuinely cares about you as a person and wants you to succeed. He is also basically omnipresent on emails, and you pretty much never have to wait more than a day. I got multiple responses from him within 10 minutes to an hour. If you have to reschedule a quiz, he basically leaves it up to your TA. His TAs are chill, so this is completely fine. He is very willing to let you reschedule exams in a timely manner, even if you don't provide documentation. I was having a breakdown with 4 exams in a single week, and he didn't miss a beat, replying in like 10 minutes, accepting my requests without any pushback. He has more-or-less weekly quizzes and worksheets. Worksheets are graded on effort, so just do them and try each question, and he'll give you a 100. If you can't make it to class, just email him, and he'll send you the worksheet and have you email it to your TA. I've never gotten anything less than 100 in his class, but from what I've heard, he is very generous with partial credit if you make a small algebra mistake but demonstrate that you understand the concept he taught you. He also often doesn't require you to simplify answers, which means there's less chance of making small algebraic mistakes. His exams are also extremely fair because they have way fewer questions than most other professors (usually 5-6), so it's not nearly as much of a race against the clock. He's also not trying to trick you; he gives you questions that are very similar to those on practice exams. No WebAssign or MATLAB homeworks, just suggested problems for each quiz. You don't have to do these, but you should, so you can practice for quizzes. I already learned Calculus 1 through 3 in high school, but I just didn't take the AP exams, so lectures are kind of irrelevant to me. However, from what I've heard from people who didn't, his lectures are extremely helpful. Not derivation-heavy, pretty much just examples of problems you'll have to solve. If we don't get to something, he'll adjust the quizzes accordingly, so as to ensure you don't have to study on your own.

Before I get into my review, I should note that the C+ is pretty much entirely on me. I should have taken the course more seriously, especially for the first midterm, and I got burned for not doing so. At least I passed. With that said, this class did not work for me whatsoever. It's not because the class is hard, though it absolutely is, and I'd argue it should be. I just don't think it's for the right reasons. For instance, the lecture/exam half of the course is almost entirely disjoint from the GeekOS project half of the course, and it really feels like a 5/6 credit course sometimes. Being good at the lecture content will not help you whatsoever with GeekOS, and vice versa. This seems to be a 412-wide issue. Regarding the lecture content, I don't think Pete is a very good lecturer. It's sort of what the other reviewers this semester so far have pointed out. I wouldn't quite agree with the tin can rattling mentality, but he certainly doesn't practice his presentations, and he brings absolutely no energy to the class. Another reviewer pointed out the ChatGPT image, which he said he would fix and never did, but there was another instance where he took a TRIO slide set from the internet, didn't review it at all beforehand, and tried going through it in a rather miserable showing. There's very little transformation of his slide content in his lectures, as all he does is take his laser pointer and point to things he wants to emphasize on one of the projectors in the room. The slides themselves are rather poor summaries of OSTEP, which he follows very closely. That's just lectures themselves. The assignments he gives aren't much better in my opinion. He assigns weekly Gradescope reading homeworks which are worth 1% of the grade each. I honestly almost wish he would give more traditional homeworks instead. Some of the questions are horribly ambiguous, there's no room to state any assumptions, there are some questions where it feels like even with both the slides and OSTEP you can't really answer well, they ultimately lack engagement, and they are nowhere near comprehensive enough to actually prepare for the exams imo. Regarding exams, exam 1 was insane with the short answer questions of random topics from the slides being worth so much of the grade, while exams 2 and 3, especially 3, were relatively more chill. These certainly weren't my strongsuit, as I'm horrible with memorizing topics which I haven't worked directly with in some meaningful way, and I'm rather terrible at studying. I didn't like them, but they were fine I guess. One question I would like to address is the barber shop semaphore problem in exam 2. Not only were the semantics poorly defined, as the professor admitted, but in my experience, semaphore programming isn't just something just I get right away. I haven't worked with them before, as I haven't had any need to. They really weren't gone over well in class, nor were the gradescope assignments enough to really nail it in. He didn't give any other practice problem on them besides the baboon problem from a reading homework. I realize this is just one specific example, but it's emblematic of my problem with this part of the class as a whole. I also realize this could just be me, and my review should be taken with at least a grain of salt due to my meager performance compared to the rest of the class. I didn't mention this before, but each exam was 15%, and there was no final exam. Regarding GeekOS, the TA's, especially Leo, really carried here. They were really helpful in getting some of the projects working, and I really wouldn't have passed the class without them. Though, I'd maybe argue they were a bit too necessary to get through the projects. It's very clear the project specs haven't been updated in years, and the project slides, especially for the later projects such as 4b and all of 5, don't seem at all sufficient in getting you through the projects. Of course, the projects should be challenging, but in my experience, there was a lot of frustration due to how much information the slides and specs omit. For example, in project 5, file systems, GFS3 is a completely proprietary file system, yet we're not really given a good specification of it. For example, we were only given one example GFS3 image whose structure is completely undocumented. In project 4b, demand paging (the hardest project imo, though I hated 5 more just by nature), the way in which we were basically required to do things isn't very easy to deduce from source code, and the slides honestly made it more confusing what we had to do. Don't get me wrong, these projects are pretty cool at the end of the day, and honestly it was very useful being forced to navigate and implement significant components into a Linux-like kernel. I just think the projects would be better if the provided resources were more helpful. Finally, there's grading. The class is graded on a curve. This semester, seemingly a lot of insanely smart people took the class, which seemingly skewed the grade distribution like crazy. There was a review last semester of someone getting an 88 with Dr. Agrawala and ending with an A+. I know someone who got like an 89 this semester and ended with an A-. Take that for what you will. Overall, I can't say I don't recommend taking this class at all, but I have some issues with it. Pete is teaching this class next spring, so it seems for a little bit, Dr. Agrawala and Pete are alternating teaching this class.

The projects aren't easy but they're all easier than some of the ones you do in 330, in my opinion, and that's a required course. In summary - If you just want to coast, you can do that easily. And if you want to really learn the material, this class gives you the freedom and time to do so because you don't have to stress about exams.

I want to start off by saying that Justin took a lot of feedback from this semester, and I don't think he's going to be doing 7 midterms again lol (i could be wrong). The class structure was 7 midterm exams, with your lowest score to be dropped, which he changed to two at the end of the semester, 6 projects, lowest dropped, and then a final take home which was very easy cause its open note and you have time to just check your notes for the answer (he says you wont but if you I did this and still had like 45 minutes of time to spare). Overall the lectures were really well taught, and you can tell he puts effort into thinking how to make it understandable for students. The exams were annoying since they were every two weeks, with means of ~83. Again at the end of the semester he was very gracious in taking feedback, and ended up dropping a 2nd exam. The whole semester I thought I was going to end up with an A-, but he ended up dropping the grade boundary all the way to 91, combined with the dropping of exams if you do all the projects its not too difficult to get an A. I probably would have given him a 3 star, but him taking feedback sincerely was nice so I think he deserves a 4. But still, I think he kind of went overkill with the 7 exams. This is hands down the worst course I've taken all my life, not just in college. This is more of a review for the course than the professor, Regli is chill (judging from the one time I met him). It IS a very easy class: cheat sheet, ez homeworks, broad material. Why the poor rating? The course structure, specifically the syllabus. This is a very broad class, concepts and terms are mentioned, basic parts of algorithms are taught, but you will not end up taking anything from the course. The only way for you to truly understand whats going on is if you read the book, the additional material along with the slides and visit office hours, etc. Exams seem like a test of can-you-create-the-best-cheatsheet. To me, it felt like a terminology class, does X mean this, etc. Exams being MCQs is another big factor of why this course is stupid. I should also add that this course is about GOFAI (good old fashioned AI) which means its almost entirely irrelevant to anything ML (there's minor relevance to robotics and RL, but thats it) Reasons to take this class: you want to do the ML track (which was my reason), you want an ez A Reasons not to take to class: if you care about your time/course choice or If you want to learn smth. I personally feel like unless you are solidifying your GPA, choice of 4XXs matters. I would say if do not fall in the category above, DO NOT take this class. You will genuinely learn nothing. My 8th grade art class where I never did anything but painted one canvas was more of a learning experience for me. PS: Again, Regli's chill and its the syllabus that is crap. I should add that I never went to class and only showed up for exams, so make of this review what you will (although idt attending class will help much, the material is too broad, concepts are never explained properly, its all way too rushed)

As a graduating senior, this is one of the classes that I have found most valuable to my education. The course content is high level and relevant. Class time is not wasted learning or doing things that do not matter. Lecture is where we learn, discussion is where we code together. This gives you the tools you need to complete the only assignments for the course- articles that you write and post on a topic of your choosing. What I like about this is that we will leave the class with tangible evidence of our learning that we can show off on our resume or to recruiters in the future. I can't say enough good things about this professor or this course. This is how all classes should be structured in my opinion. I highly highly recommend taking this course with Professor Buntain.

I think Teli is alright, but still a good choice for 250. He doesn't explain things very clearly, but he makes up for this by going through a lot of examples in depth during lecture. You're left with a strong understanding on how to answer questions correctly, but with hazy knowledge on why you format the steps in the way you're supposed to, especially since some of the TAs will format their proofs or answer problems a bit differently than Teli did. It's not a problem for most of the semester--the midterms are incredibly easy, easier than the practice exams. The content in the course only really gets difficult between the second midterm and the final, and since the final isn't cumulative, there's no easy content from the beginning to pad it; but still very doable if you study well. The quizzes are sometimes easy, sometimes difficult--definitely study for those, especially as you get further into the semester. Homeworks are challenging, so don't slack off on those either. Overall, the negatives of his lecturing style don't really show themselves until you reach the end of the course, and even then just skimming the recommended textbook helps solidify the things he doesn't go over as much. I complain about his lecturing style a lot, but honestly he is a solid choice for 250 and I would recommend; put in the work, and it's not difficult to get an A.

My review won't be as critical as the other one for this semester, but I share a lot of the sentiments about Pete and the class. Pete himself admitted that his info about this topic in general is out of date one class, and his generally subpar lecturing style (very monotone) leads to a lot of confusion and difficulty understanding content. We follow an online (free) textbook which goes into more detail, but a lot of the content on the exams is either difficult to find in the textbook or just something he put on a couple slides. The exams themselves aren't difficult given you scour the slides and your notes. All the problems on the exam are either short form questions about certain topics or definitions, or questions you've seen before on homeworks. The projects are on the more difficult side compared to other 4XX classes, and set up similar to 417 where they're tangentially related to what we're currently learning about in class, but most of the work is figuring out how to implement the features within the existing GeekOS system. I personally really enjoyed these projects, they were interesting and fun to work with. The difference though between this class and 417 though, is that the project specs are rather useless. They don't really help much with understanding what you're doing at all to be honest, and its hard to get a grasp of the scope of each project purely from the spec sheets. It's not impossible, but there's a noticeable difference that leads to a worse experience. However, the issues with projects is all offset by the TA Leo. For every project, he provided a video and slides that allowed us to work our way through each project step by step. He gave us good tips and ideas during OH, and basically led the project part of the course.

Solely judging on how "easy" the class is, I would give it a 4 stars. The buffer overflows project was the only extremely difficult one, the other's just took some time, but nothing crazy. In terms of how much I learned, I would give this class a 2 stars. I will say, I actually went to lecture 75% of the time so I probably got more out of the class than people who never went so that's on them. Marsh's teaching style was ... alright. I think a flipped classroom CAN work, but I don't think it was the best in this case, especially given the fact that there was SOOOO much content. (I also just find it really hard to focus when watching videos). I don't agree with the reviews, below, it really was not that bad. Some of the quizzes were a little confusing, but you had unlimited attempts at them. His grading scale was also incredibly fair (he used a EMRN scale for writing instead of grading with numbers), and as long as you started the work before it was due, it was pretty manageable. I believe he's planning on removing the late deadlines, but this is probably a good thing. I know a lot of people let work pile up at the end of the semester and it hurt their grade. The group project SUCKED, but mostly because I had a terrible group who waited until a week before it was due to even look at the project. The instructions were a little confusing but if you spoke with a TA or Marsh early it made a bit more sense. It wasn't necessarily hard, just a bit confusing on what we were supposed to protect against. There were also no exams which was a huge bonus in my opinion. I started the semester seriously freaked out about this class, but after I figured out the buffer overflows project, which admittedly took me forever, I found the rest to be pretty easy. Everyone says this but just start the projects early and speak to TAs or Marsh when you get stuck, it really helps.

I honestly think Professor Rudinger deserves a higher rating. Starting with the good: The lectures were interesting and informative, offering clear explanations of complex topics. Professor Rudinger was very helpful during office hours and genuinely cared about students’ understanding. HWs and exams are not difficult, and I felt that they reflected the course content well. Also, the new grading structure (gone is the 45% final, its weight split between an additional midterm and final) was a positive change, making the overall grade distribution more balanced. Formula sheets were allowed for every exam, which was helpful. However, there are still quite a few areas for improvement: Students’ questions on Piazza often went unanswered for days. He's not a bad teacher for CMSC411. You don't study a lot of material in this class, but you're expected to know the concepts you are taught like the back of your hand. We had 3 exams (including the final) worth about 16% of your grade each. I thought all were very fair, which surprised me. The only tricky part was the T/F which tested you on a bunch of technicalities. There were 2 projects, both written in C. However, I thought the projects had no business being in C, as everything you simulate and implement could have been done in Python or any other high-level language to avoid the hassle that comes with low-level programming. The 5 homeworks were fine. They took me on average 3 hours each and I averaged an 88 on them. Overall, I wouldn't urge you to not take his class, but I wouldn't suggest scrambling to get a seat in it. -1 stars for the projects being a little unorganized, and -1 for sort of dry course content. Nothing bad to say about Dr. Yoon himself.

Just a note about the really bad warnings: we were only told that he was switching his class format about two weeks before the semester started so I would guess that some people who were really unhappy may not have had enough time to find a new class or realized what 7 exams would entail for them (especially poor test takers). Yes, 7 exams could be stressful (this is the reason I deducted a star, but really I'd give a 4.5 if possible). However, the exams were really fair except for the first one. They were a lot like the recommended problems, some of them were even directly from these problems. For anyone who doesn't struggle with serious test anxiety, you'll probably be fine. Do the recommended problems and try to stay on top of content so you don't have to cram for each exam. Justin himself is a great teacher. His lectures were pretty engaging and he explained things really well. The only real complaint I have about the exams is that sometimes the proofs were just a little too difficult for someone who isn't used to proofs. The first exam was kind of heinous, but I think Justin just didn't account for the fact that it had been awhile since we had seen 351 material and we all had professors who taught the content differently. And Justin is INCREDIBLY nice, like way nicer than a professor really has to be. He wasn't out to get us with the 7 exam thing, he was just trying to make the course fair to those of us who refuse to cheat on every single assignment handed to us. He dropped an extra exam after seeing how much stress some of the students were experiencing due to the change in class structure. He extended project deadlines MULTIPLE times. Again, as long as you're not someone who has serious test anxiety you will do fine.
